title: Isolated Converters
description: Transformers in switching converters: the magnetizing-inductance model, flyback, forward, bridge and push-pull converters, turns ratios and transformer reset.

study.title: Why isolation?
study.body: A transformer between input and output gives **galvanic isolation** (safety for mains-powered supplies, separate grounds), allows **large voltage ratios** without extreme duty cycles (a buck from 400 V to 5 V would need $D$ = 1.25 %), and makes **multiple outputs** easy with extra windings. Each isolated converter is a basic converter with a transformer inserted; its ratio gets an extra factor $n = N_s/N_p$.

study.title: Transformer model
study.body: Model a real transformer as an ideal one plus a **magnetizing inductance** $L_M$ across the primary (and a small leakage inductance in series). $L_M$ is a real inductor: it obeys volt-second balance, so the primary voltage must average to zero over a period. Otherwise the magnetizing current, and with it the core flux, grows every period until the core **saturates**.

study.title: The flyback converter
study.body: A buck-boost whose inductor got a second winding: $L_M$ is the energy store. $Q_1$ on: $V_g$ across the primary, $i_M$ rises, and the opposite dots keep $D_1$ reverse biased. $Q_1$ off: the winding voltages reverse, $D_1$ conducts and the stored energy flows to the output. $Q_1$ must block $V_g$ plus the reflected output voltage $V/n$.

study.title: The forward converter
study.body: A buck with a transformer. $Q_1$ on: the secondary delivers $nV_g$, $D_2$ conducts and $L$ charges. $Q_1$ off: $D_3$ freewheels the inductor current, as in a buck. So $V = nDV_g$. The transformer stores no useful energy, but its magnetizing current must be **reset** every period, usually by a third winding $N_r$ that returns the magnetizing energy to the input (not drawn).

study.title: Transformer reset
study.body: With a reset winding the primary voltage is $V_g$ for $DT_s$ and $-V_gN_p/N_r$ while the core resets. Volt-second balance gives a reset time $D_2T_s = DT_sN_r/N_p$, which must fit before the next turn-on: $D + D_2 \le 1$. With $N_r = N_p$ (the usual choice) $D \le 0.5$ and $Q_1$ must block $2V_g$. The volt-seconds also set the peak-to-peak flux-density swing, $2\Delta B = V_gDT_s/(N_pA_c)$ ($\Delta B$, like $\Delta i_L$, is half the swing).

study.title: Bridge and push-pull converters
study.body: For higher power the transformer is driven in both directions. A **full bridge** (four switches) applies $+V_g$, 0, $-V_g$, 0 to the primary; each half of the transformer period the rectified secondary is $nV_g$ for a fraction $D$, so $V = nDV_g$. Switches block only $V_g$, and the core flux swings both ways (better use of the core). The **half bridge** applies $\pm V_g/2$ and needs only two switches. The **push-pull** uses a center-tapped primary; its two switches must block $2V_g$.
study.formula: \begin{aligned}& V = nDV_g\quad\text{(full bridge, push-pull)}\\ & V = \tfrac12 nDV_g\quad\text{(half bridge)}\end{aligned}

study.title: Worked example: flyback
study.body:
$V_g$ = 48 V, $V$ = 12 V at 2 A, $N_p : N_s$ = 2 : 1 ($n$ = 0.5).
- $\frac{D}{1-D} = \frac{V}{nV_g}$ = 12/24 = 0.5, so $D$ = 1/3.
- $Q_1$ blocks $V_g + V/n$ = 48 + 24 = 72 V; $D_1$ blocks $V + nV_g$ = 12 + 24 = 36 V.
- Primary-referred magnetizing current: $I_M = nI_{out}/D'$ = 0.5 × 2 / (2/3) = 1.5 A. Check: $P_{in} = V_g D I_M$ = 48 × (1/3) × 1.5 = 24 W = $P_{out}$.

steps.title: The transformer in a converter
steps.body: Treat the transformer as an ideal one (voltages scale with $n = N_s/N_p$) plus a magnetizing inductance $L_M$ across the primary. While the primary has $V_g$ across it, the magnetizing current ramps up with slope $V_g/L_M$, exactly like the current in any inductor.

steps.prompt: An ideal transformer stores energy and releases it later in the switching period.
steps.explanation: An ideal transformer has infinite $L_M$: it passes power from primary to secondary instantly and stores nothing. Only the magnetizing inductance stores energy. The forward converter tries to keep that energy small; the flyback uses $L_M$ deliberately as its energy store.

steps.prompt: A transformer primary with $L_M$ = {{LM|H}} sees {{Vg|V}} for {{D*100}} % of each {{fs|Hz}} period. By how much does the magnetizing current rise (peak-to-peak)?
steps.explanation: $2\Delta i_M = \frac{V_g}{L_M}DT_s$ = {{Vg}} V × {{D/fs|s}} / {{LM|H}} = **{{Vg*D/(fs*LM)|A}}**.

steps.title: The flyback converter
steps.body: $Q_1$ on: $V_g$ magnetizes $L_M$; because the dots are on opposite ends, the secondary voltage reverse-biases $D_1$ and the output capacitor feeds the load. $Q_1$ off: the magnetizing current transfers to the secondary, $D_1$ conducts and the energy goes to the output. It is a buck-boost with a turns ratio, so $V = nV_gD/D'$ (positive here thanks to the winding polarity).

steps.prompt: A flyback converter with $N_p : N_s$ = {{k}} : 1 runs from {{Vg|V}} at $D$ = {{D}} (CCM). Find the output voltage.
Why are the dots of a flyback transformer on **opposite** ends of the two windings?
options: So that $D_1$ blocks while $Q_1$ is on and conducts after $Q_1$ turns off
So that power flows to the output while $Q_1$ is on
steps.explanation: With opposite dots, $Q_1$ on makes the diode end of the secondary negative, so no secondary current flows and $L_M$ stores energy. When $Q_1$ turns off, all winding voltages reverse and the magnetizing current continues through the secondary and $D_1$. That two-step energy transfer is what makes it a flyback (buck-boost) rather than a forward (buck) converter.

steps.prompt: A flyback converter makes {{V|V}} from {{Vg|V}} with $N_p : N_s$ = {{k}} : 1. What voltage must the MOSFET block while it is off (ignore leakage spikes)?
steps.explanation: With $D_1$ conducting the secondary has $V$ across it, which reflects to the primary as $V\cdot N_p/N_s$ = {{k}} × {{V|V}} = {{k*V|V}}. The drain sits at $V_g$ plus this: **{{Vg+k*V|V}}**. In practice the leakage inductance adds a spike on top, so a clamp or snubber and extra margin are needed.

steps.prompt: A flyback converter with $N_p : N_s$ = {{k}} : 1 must make {{V|V}} from {{Vg|V}}. What duty cycle does it need (CCM)?
steps.explanation: $\frac{D}{1-D} = \frac{V}{nV_g} = \frac{N_p}{N_s}\cdot\frac{V}{V_g}$ = {{k}} × {{V}} / {{Vg}} = {{k*V/Vg||3}} → $D = \frac{(N_p/N_s)V}{V_g + (N_p/N_s)V}$ = **{{k*V/(Vg+k*V)||3}}**.

steps.title: The forward converter
steps.body: While $Q_1$ is on, the secondary delivers $nV_g$ through $D_2$ to an LC filter, exactly like a buck's switch node. When $Q_1$ is off, $D_3$ carries the inductor current. The output inductor sees $nV_g - V$ and $-V$, so volt-second balance gives $V = nDV_g$.

steps.prompt: A forward converter with $N_p : N_s$ = {{k}} : 1 runs from {{Vg|V}} at $D$ = {{D}}. Find $V$.
A forward converter must make {{V|V}} from {{Vg|V}} at a duty cycle of {{D}}. What turns ratio $N_p/N_s$ does it need?

steps.title: Resetting the core
steps.body: While $Q_1$ is on, $i_M$ ramps up. After turn-off the magnetizing current flows through the reset winding back into $V_g$, which puts $-V_gN_p/N_r$ across the primary until $i_M$ is zero. A larger $N_r$ means a lower reset voltage (less switch stress) but a longer reset, so a lower maximum duty cycle.

steps.prompt: A forward converter's reset winding has $N_r/N_p$ = {{r}}, and $V_g$ = {{Vg|V}}.

ask.prompt: What is the maximum duty cycle?
What voltage must $Q_1$ block during reset?
ask.explanation: During reset the primary has $-V_gN_p/N_r$ = −{{Vg/r|V}} across it, so the drain is at $V_g + V_gN_p/N_r$ = {{Vg}} × (1 + 1/{{r}}) = **{{Vg*(1+1/r)|V}}**.

steps.prompt: In a forward converter, energy is stored in the transformer while $Q_1$ is on and delivered to the output after it turns off.
steps.explanation: That is the flyback. In the forward converter power flows straight through the transformer while $Q_1$ is on; the output **inductor** does the energy storage, as in a buck. The (small) magnetizing energy is returned to the input through the reset winding.

steps.prompt: A forward converter runs at $D$ = {{D}}. The graph shows the magnetizing current over one period for a reset winding ratio $N_r/N_p$. Choose the **largest** ratio that still resets the core before the next turn-on.
steps.explanation: Reset lasts $D_2T_s = D\frac{N_r}{N_p}T_s$; it must end by $t = T_s$: $D(1 + N_r/N_p) = 1$ → $N_r/N_p = \frac{1-D}{D}$ = **{{(1-D)/D||3}}**. The switch then blocks $V_g(1 + N_p/N_r) = \frac{V_g}{1-D}$ = {{1/(1-D)||3}}$V_g$, the lowest possible stress at this duty cycle.

steps.prompt: A forward transformer has $N_p$ = {{Np}} turns on a core with $A_c$ = {{Ac*1e6}} mm². It runs from {{Vg|V}} at $D$ = {{D}} and {{fs|Hz}}. What is the peak-to-peak flux-density swing $2\Delta B$?
steps.explanation: Volt-seconds: $\lambda = V_gDT_s$ = {{Vg*D/fs|V}}·s. $2\Delta B = \frac{\lambda}{N_pA_c}$ = {{Vg*D/fs}} / ({{Np}} × {{Ac}} m²) = **{{Vg*D/(fs*Np*Ac)|T}}**. Ferrites saturate around 0.3–0.4 T, so a forward converter keeps the swing well below that (core loss at high $f_s$ limits it further).

steps.title: Full bridge, half bridge, push-pull
steps.body:
- **Full bridge**: four switches apply $\pm V_g$ to the primary; $V = nDV_g$; switches block $V_g$.
- **Half bridge**: a capacitive divider gives $\pm V_g/2$; $V = \frac12 nDV_g$; switches block $V_g$.
- **Push-pull**: two switches on a center-tapped primary; $V = nDV_g$; switches block $2V_g$.
Here $D$ is the fraction of each half-period in which the rectified secondary voltage is non-zero.

steps.prompt: A full-bridge converter with $N_p : N_s$ = {{k}} : 1 runs from {{Vg|V}} with $D$ = {{D}}. Find the output voltage.
A half-bridge converter must make {{V|V}} from {{Vg|V}} at $D$ = {{D}}. What turns ratio $N_p/N_s$ does it need?
steps.explanation: The primary only sees $\pm V_g/2$: $V = \frac{N_s}{N_p}D\frac{V_g}{2}$ → $\frac{N_p}{N_s} = \frac{DV_g}{2V}$ = {{D}} × {{Vg}} / (2 × {{V}}) = **{{D*Vg/(2*V)||3}}**.

steps.prompt: A push-pull converter runs from {{Vg|V}}. What voltage must each of its switches block (ignoring spikes)?
steps.explanation: When one switch conducts, $V_g$ is across its half of the primary; by transformer action the other half also has $V_g$ across it, adding to the supply. The off switch therefore sees **{{2*Vg|V}}**, which is why push-pull suits low input voltages.

steps.prompt: Match each isolated converter to its key feature
pairs: Energy stored in L_M; no output inductor
Needs a reset winding; D ≤ 0.5 when N_r = N_p
Four switches; best for high power
steps.explanation: Flybacks are the simplest (one switch, one diode per output) and dominate below ~100 W. Forward converters handle more power with a single switch but need core reset. Bridges use the core in both directions and keep switch stress at $V_g$, so they dominate at kilowatts. Push-pull suits low-voltage inputs.

steps.prompt: You want to step {{Vg|V}} down to {{V|V}}.

ask.prompt: With a plain buck at {{fs|Hz}}, how long would the on-time be?
ask.explanation: $D = V/V_g$ = {{V/Vg||3}}, so $t_{on} = DT_s$ = {{V/Vg||3}} × {{1/fs|s}} = **{{V/(Vg*fs)|s}}**: too short to control accurately, and the switch would need a {{Vg|V}} rating while carrying the full output current.

ask.prompt: A full-bridge converter should run at $D$ = 0.7 instead. What $N_p/N_s$ does that need?
ask.explanation: $V = \frac{N_s}{N_p}DV_g$ → $\frac{N_p}{N_s} = \frac{0.7\,V_g}{V}$ = 0.7 × {{Vg}} / {{V}} = **{{0.7*Vg/V||3}}**. The transformer does the bulk of the step-down.

steps.prompt: Flyback converters are popular for low-power, multi-output supplies partly because each output needs only a winding, a diode and a capacitor.
steps.explanation: The magnetizing inductance is the only energy store, so no output inductor is needed. Adding an output costs one winding, one diode and one capacitor. The price: high peak currents and switch stress, which limit flybacks to roughly 100 W and below.

steps.prompt: A flyback converter runs from {{Vg|V}} and must make {{V|V}}. The MOSFET is rated {{Vds|V}} and you allow at most 80 % of that in steady state (leakage spikes need the rest). What is the largest turns ratio $N_p/N_s$ you can use?
steps.explanation: Off-state drain voltage: $V_g + \frac{N_p}{N_s}V \le 0.8\,V_{DS}$ = {{0.8*Vds|V}}. So $\frac{N_p}{N_s} \le \frac{0.8V_{DS} - V_g}{V}$ = ({{0.8*Vds}} − {{Vg}}) / {{V}} = **{{(0.8*Vds-Vg)/V||3}}**.

steps.prompt: A CCM flyback converter runs from {{Vgmin|V}} to {{Vgmax|V}} and makes {{V|V}}. Its turns ratio is chosen so that the duty cycle reaches its limit of 0.5 at the lowest input voltage.

ask.prompt: What is the duty cycle at the highest input voltage?
ask.explanation: $N_p/N_s$ = {{k||3}}, so the reflected output voltage is $\frac{N_p}{N_s}V$ = {{k*V|V}}. $D = \frac{(N_p/N_s)V}{V_{g,max} + (N_p/N_s)V}$ = {{k*V}} / ({{Vgmax}} + {{k*V}}) = **{{k*V/(Vgmax+k*V)||3}}**.

ask.prompt: What is the MOSFET's off-state voltage at the highest input voltage?

steps.prompt: A CCM flyback converter: $V_g$ = {{Vg|V}}, $D$ = {{D}}, $N_p : N_s$ = {{k}} : 1, output current {{Io|A}}, $L_M$ = {{LM|H}}, $f_s$ = {{fs|Hz}}.

ask.prompt: What is the average magnetizing current (referred to the primary)?
ask.explanation: During $D'T_s$ the secondary carries $i_M N_p/N_s$ = {{k}}$\,i_M$, and its average must equal $I_{out}$: $D'\frac{N_p}{N_s}I_M = I_{out}$ → $I_M = \frac{I_{out}}{(N_p/N_s)(1-D)}$ = {{Io}} / ({{k}} × {{1-D||2}}) = **{{IM|A}}**.

ask.prompt: What is the peak MOSFET current?

steps.prompt: A single-switch forward converter ($N_r = N_p$) runs from {{Vgmin|V}} to {{Vgmax|V}} and makes {{V|V}}. Design for $D$ = 0.45 at the lowest input.

ask.prompt: What is the duty cycle at the highest input?
What is the worst-case MOSFET off-state voltage?
ask.explanation: With $N_r = N_p$ the reset voltage equals $V_g$, so the switch blocks $2V_g$, worst at $V_{g,max}$: 2 × {{Vgmax}} = **{{2*Vgmax|V}}**. That is why off-line forward converters often use the two-switch variant, whose switches only block $V_g$.

steps.prompt: A flyback converter makes {{V|V}} from {{Vg|V}} with $N_p : N_s$ = {{k}} : 1. What reverse voltage must the output diode block while $Q_1$ is on?
steps.explanation: With $Q_1$ on, the secondary carries $V_g N_s/N_p$ = {{Vg/k|V}} with the polarity that drives the diode's anode negative, while its cathode sits at $+V$. Reverse voltage: $V + V_gN_s/N_p$ = **{{V+Vg/k|V}}**.

steps.prompt: Doubling the magnetizing inductance of a CCM flyback converter halves the magnetizing current ripple but leaves its average value unchanged.
steps.explanation: The average $I_M = \frac{I_{out}}{(N_p/N_s)D'}$ comes from charge balance and does not involve $L_M$. The ripple $2\Delta i_M = V_gDT_s/L_M$ is inversely proportional to $L_M$. A larger $L_M$ lowers the peak current but needs a bigger core.

steps.prompt: A forward transformer runs from {{Vg|V}} at $D_{max}$ = {{D}} and {{fs|Hz}}. The core has $A_c$ = {{Ac*1e6}} mm² and the peak-to-peak flux-density swing must stay below {{Bm}} T. What is the minimum number of primary turns (round up)?
steps.explanation: $N_p \ge \frac{V_gDT_s}{2\Delta B\,A_c}$ = {{Vg*D/fs}} V·s / ({{Bm}} T × {{Ac}} m²) = {{Vg*D/(fs*Bm*Ac)||3}}, so **{{ceil(Vg*D/(fs*Bm*Ac))}} turns**.

steps.prompt: Put the events of one flyback switching period in order, starting at turn-on.
items: Q_1 turns on and V_g appears across the primary
The magnetizing current ramps up; D_1 is reverse biased
Q_1 turns off; the winding voltages reverse and D_1 starts to conduct
The leakage-inductance energy causes a short drain-voltage spike, absorbed by the clamp
The magnetizing energy flows to the output while i_M ramps down
steps.explanation: Energy is first stored in $L_M$ (diode off), then released to the output (switch off). The leakage inductance does not couple to the secondary: its current cannot transfer to $D_1$, so right after turn-off it drives a short voltage spike that a clamp or snubber must absorb. For the rest of the off-time the stored magnetizing energy flows to the output.
